01.actor: a blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
01.event: One day he was late; Shmuel sent a messenger, who missed him on the road, reached his house and reported that his wife had committed adultery
01.turn: The blind man brings the report to Mar Shmuel
01.outcome: Shmuel rules: if you trust him, divorce her; if not, do not
01.summary: A blind man who used to review mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day. Shmuel sent a messenger after him; they passed each other on different roads, and the messenger, arriving at the house, saw the man's wife committing adultery and reported it. The blind man came to Shmuel, who told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger and not otherwise.
01.reason: A one-time event with several narrated actions (lateness, sending, missing each other, the discovery, coming to the rabbi) before the ruling; this is R-C0's incident-plus-ruling, with more than coming before a rabbi.

02.event: He is asked the halakha on the rival wife of a daughter
02.turn: He refuses to decide between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, fearing for his skull
02.outcome: He testifies that families descended from rival wives produced High Priests
02.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua was asked about the rival wife of a daughter and said it was disputed between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Pressed for the ruling, he declined, saying he feared the two great mountains would crush his head, but testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives and produced High Priests.
02.missing: Any event beyond the question and his answer; the testimony is a report, not something that happens in the passage
02.reason: A question and answer with a testimony about past practice; no event beyond speech and no conflict beyond ordinary halakhic discourse.

03.event: He tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would become angry
03.outcome: Not told in the passage; the Gemara only analyzes the permissibility of the test
03.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether Rabba would become angry. The Gemara then asks how he could risk causing his son to sin, and answers that he had forgone his honor.
03.missing: The son's reaction and any outcome of the test
03.reason: There is one real act with a purpose (a test), but the passage cites it as precedent and gives no response or outcome; the rest is Gemara analysis. Between a bare report and a story, so borderline.

04.event: He found the residents of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in a synagogue and told them to place it farther in
04.outcome: Rava says no one follows Rabbi Akiva on this
04.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon the people of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in a synagogue and instructed them to put it farther in to gain more distance. Rava rebuked him as argumentative, saying nobody follows Rabbi Akiva's view on eiruvin.
04.missing: Any action following the instruction or the rebuke
04.reason: A setting that frames a ruling, then a rebuke; the rebuke is ordinary Talmudic discourse and nothing changes.

05.missing: A one-time event; the passage describes Rava's habitual ruling practice
05.reason: A custom of how Rava would rule when people came before him, leading to no narrated event or change.

06.event: He saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat and shouted at him
06.turn: The man ignored him, and Ravina declared him excommunicated in his teacher's presence
06.outcome: Ravina asks whether this was irreverent; Rav Ashi approves, since where God's name is desecrated no honor is paid to a teacher
06.summary: While sitting before Rav Ashi, Ravina saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. He shouted at him, the man paid no attention, and Ravina declared him excommunicated. Afterwards he asked Rav Ashi whether that had been disrespectful, and Rav Ashi told him that where God's name is desecrated, no honor is paid to a teacher.
06.reason: Several narrated actions (the violation, the shout, the man ignoring it, the excommunication) with conflict and a resolution.

07.event: He went as an agent to betroth a woman to his son
07.turn: He betrothed her to himself instead, because her family would not give her to the son
07.outcome: He did not tell his son first, fearing someone else would betroth her in the meantime
07.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman for his son but ended up betrothing her to himself. The Gemara explains that the family refused the son, and that he acted at once because he feared someone else would take her while he went back to tell his son.
07.reason: Two actions and a change: sent to do one thing, he does another. The Gemara's justifications are commentary, but the core incident is narrated.

08.missing: Anything beyond a single act (a betrothal with silk) followed by an amoraic dispute
08.reason: One event and then legal discussion with nothing changing afterward; under R-C0 as of 2026-10-25 this is not a story.

09.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
09.event: Rav Yosef says he never heard a halakha; Abaye reminds him he taught it to them
09.turn: Rav Yosef remembers and corrects the wording Abaye attributed to him
09.outcome: He restates his teaching about partitions
09.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a teaching of Shmuel about roofs. Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it to them, quoting him. Rav Yosef then recalled it and corrected the version Abaye had given.
09.missing: Any event beyond the exchange; the illness behind his forgetting is only in the translator's gloss
09.reason: All dialogue about a halakha, with no conflict beyond ordinary scholarly back-and-forth and no event beyond speech.

10.event: He boasts that he is like ben Azzai, ready for any question
10.turn: A Sage asks him how many apples make an eiruv
10.outcome: Rava answers with a counter-question; the exchange continues outside the passage
10.summary: Rava declared he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias. One of the Sages asked him how many apples are needed for an eiruv, and Rava replied, does one make an eiruv with apples?
10.missing: Any event beyond speech, and the outcome of the challenge
10.reason: A boast and a question and answer; a challenge of this kind is ordinary Talmudic dialogue, and nothing happens beyond speaking.

11.event: The reservoir at Yavne, presumed complete, was measured and found deficient
11.turn: Tarfon declares the past immersions pure, Akiva impure; they argue with parables until Akiva distinguishes the cases
11.outcome: Tarfon concedes: whoever separates from you separates from life
11.summary: The ritual bath at Yavne, presumed full, was measured and found short. Rabbi Tarfon held that the purifications done in it were valid and Rabbi Akiva that they were not; each argued from a parable. Rabbi Akiva then analyzed which parable fit, and Rabbi Tarfon accepted his reasoning and praised him.
11.missing: Narrated action after the discovery; the rest is legal argument
11.reason: One real event (the measurement) followed mostly by legal debate, but with conflict between the sages and a change (Tarfon persuaded); mainly speech with something happening, so borderline rather than not.

12.event: He immigrates to Eretz Yisrael, is ordained, and is appointed to the intercalation council
12.turn: At each step he declares himself spared one more of Ezekiel's curses
12.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was seated on the council for intercalating the calendar he said three.
12.reason: Three narrated events about a sage with clear change in his status and his response to each; more than speech or a report.

13.missing: Any event; the passage only mentions a balcony that Abaye and Rava disputed all their lives
13.reason: A lifelong disagreement cited as evidence, with no narrated action or change; it is legal discussion, not an incident.

14.event: He arrived at Apsetaya and forbade climbing even a stripped tree
14.outcome: The Gemara explains it as a protective fence
14.summary: Rav came to Apsetaya and prohibited climbing even a stripped tree. The Gemara explains that he found an unguarded place and made a fence.
14.missing: Any second event or consequence beyond the arrival and the ruling
14.reason: A visit that only frames a ruling; under the Shabbat 147a ruling a setting plus a ruling is not a story.

15.event: Serving drinks at his son's wedding, he poured for four sages; two stood before him and two did not
15.outcome: He rebuked them: are these Sages and those not Sages?
15.summary: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks himself. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua stood for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinhas son of Rav Hisda did not. Rava became angry and rebuked them.
15.reason: A one-time event with several actions, a slight, an emotional reaction (which counts as an event) and conflict.

16.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana
16.event: Mar Yehuda finds them at the door of Rabba's study hall and poses a contradiction
16.turn: They fall silent and go to Rabba
16.outcome: Rabba calls Mar Yehuda quarrelsome and resolves the contradiction
16.summary: Mar Yehuda found two sages standing at the entrance to Rabba's study hall and challenged them with a contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's view. They had no answer and went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome man had put them up to it and resolved the difficulty.
16.missing: Events beyond the scholarly exchange; the silence and going to Rabba are the only movement
16.reason: Mainly speech and scholarly challenge, but something does happen (they are stumped and go to Rabba); between borderline and not, so borderline.

17.event: He was avoiding his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wanted to move to Eretz Yisrael
17.outcome: Not told in the passage; it moves to Rav Yehuda's reason
17.summary: Rabbi Zeira kept out of sight of his teacher Rav Yehuda, because he wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael and Rav Yehuda held that leaving Babylonia was forbidden.
17.missing: Any event that follows the avoidance; the passage gives only the situation and the halakhic reason
17.reason: A real ongoing situation with implied conflict between student and teacher, but nothing follows within the passage; between a bare report and a story, so borderline.

18.event: He used to send a pauper four dinars every Shabbat eve; one day he sent them by his wife
18.turn: She came back saying the man did not need it, having heard his household ask whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths
18.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responds with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should be grateful to swindlers
18.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a poor man four dinars before Shabbat. One day he sent his wife, who returned saying the man did not need charity, since she had heard his household asking whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina answered with Rabbi Elazar's teaching that we should appreciate swindlers, who save us from sinning every day.
18.reason: A habit followed by a one-time event, a discovery and a response. Segments 4-18 are baraitot, a Mishnah and legal discussion, not part of the story.

19.actor: a man claiming to be from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
19.event: The man tells the Sages where he is from
19.turn: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stands and declares that Shot Mishot lies between the rivers
19.outcome: The Gemara discusses the lineage status and geography of that region
19.summary: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha rose and said that place lies between the rivers, and the Gemara explains that this region counts as Babylonia for lineage and discusses its borders.
19.missing: Any event beyond a statement and a pronouncement
19.reason: A statement and a ruling on lineage followed by legal-geographic discussion; no conflict and nothing changes.

20.missing: Anything beyond a report of one act by Rabbi Akiva cited as evidence
20.reason: This is Rabbi Akiva's etrog, which the editor ruled is just a report of what he did, with no continuation.
